attempts.answer_text:
The key point is: the second 10-second kill request can shorten the remaining termination deadline, but it does not restart termination from zero or replace the already-running termination operation. The pod worker keeps the original termination start time and recalculates the remaining grace period.

This behavior is implemented in pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go at Kubernetes commit 400031d69530e018d5c001a922d3c5d2afaba954.

1. First kill: 60 seconds

When the first kill request arrives, UpdatePod() sees that termination has not yet been requested:
if !status.IsTerminationRequested() {
    ...
    case options.UpdateType == kubetypes.SyncPodKill:
        ...
        status.terminatingAt = now
        becameTerminating = true
}

So the worker records terminatingAt once, at the time the pod first enters termination. Its WorkType() consequently changes from SyncPod to TerminatingPod.

The worker also maintains:

terminatingAt — when termination was requested

gracePeriod — effective grace period

startedTerminating — whether the worker has actually begun the terminating phase

terminatedAt — set only after SyncTerminatingPod succeeds

These fields are the pod worker's state machine.

2. The second kill does not reset terminatingAt

When the 10-second request arrives, this condition is now false:

if !status.IsTerminationRequested()

because terminatingAt is already populated.

Therefore Kubernetes does not execute the "begin termination" transition again. Instead it reaches:

case status.IsTerminationRequested():

and treats the request as another update to an already-terminating pod.

This distinction is important: the clock continues to run from the original termination request.

3. The 10-second request is considered for the effective grace period

Inside the terminating branch, Kubernetes calls:

calculateEffectiveGracePeriod(
    status,
    pod,
    options.KillPodOptions,
)

and then stores the result in:

status.gracePeriod = gracePeriod

It also writes the calculated value back into the kill options:

options.KillPodOptions.PodTerminationGracePeriodSecondsOverride = &gracePeriod

The source explicitly describes this as allowing the grace period to decrease while termination is in progress.

The activeUpdate state is also important here. Kubernetes describes it as the source of truth for the pod worker and explicitly says that kill options are accumulated because "pods cannot have their grace period shortened" in the ordinary accumulation path.

There is an important nuance, though: the effective grace-period calculation accounts for the elapsed time since terminatingAt. Therefore the requested 10 seconds is not interpreted as "10 seconds from the second kill request."

Conceptually:

termination began
      │
      │<--------- elapsed time --------->│
      │                                  │
      ▼                                  ▼
terminatingAt                     second kill: 10s
      │
      └── effective remaining time is calculated

So if 7 seconds have already elapsed when the 10-second request arrives, the pod has roughly 3 seconds remaining, not 10 seconds.

If more than 10 seconds have already elapsed, the effective grace period is effectively at the termination deadline rather than giving the pod another 10 seconds.

4. What happens to the in-progress SyncTerminatingPod?

This is the particularly important control-flow branch.

After the new update is placed into pendingUpdate, Kubernetes checks:

if (becameTerminating || wasGracePeriodShortened) && status.cancelFn != nil {
    ...
}

So if the new 10-second request actually shortens the effective grace period, wasGracePeriodShortened becomes true and the existing pod-sync operation can be cancelled/restarted so that the shorter deadline can take effect.

That does not mean the pod goes back to SyncPod.

Instead, the worker remains in the terminating state and reconciles toward the new effective deadline.

The podSyncer contract explicitly describes SyncTerminatingPod as something that is repeatedly invoked with diminishing grace periods, and says cancellation is allowed when a shorter grace period is detected.

5. The state transition looks like this
FIRST KILL
                 60s
                  │
                  ▼
        ┌────────────────────┐
        │ terminatingAt = T0 │
        │ gracePeriod = 60   │
        └─────────┬──────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
          TerminatingPod
                  │
                  │ SyncTerminatingPod
                  │ running
                  │
       SECOND KILL ARRIVES
              override=10
                  │
                  ▼
        already terminating
                  │
                  ▼
    calculateEffectiveGracePeriod()
                  │
                  ▼
       shorter effective deadline
                  │
                  ▼
       wasGracePeriodShortened=true
                  │
                  ▼
       cancel current sync operation
                  │
                  ▼
     rerun/reconcile termination
       using shorter remaining
            grace period
                  │
                  ▼
        containers stopped
                  │
                  ▼
        terminatedAt = now
                  │
                  ▼
          TerminatedPod
                  │
                  ▼
       shorter effective deadline
                  │
                  ▼
       wasGracePeriodShortened=true
                  │
                  ▼
       cancel current sync operation
                  │
                  ▼
     rerun/reconcile termination
       using shorter remaining
            grace period
                  │
                  ▼
        containers stopped
                  │
                  ▼
        terminatedAt = now
                  │
                  ▼
          TerminatedPod

Bottom line

For a pod that started termination with 60 seconds, then receives a 10-second kill request:

terminatingAt is not reset.

The pod stays in TerminatingPod; it does not return to SyncPod.

The second request is processed through the already-terminating branch.

Kubernetes calculates a new effective grace period using the existing termination state and elapsed time.

The effective deadline can therefore become shorter.

If it was shortened, wasGracePeriodShortened causes the currently running termination operation to be cancelled so it can observe the shorter deadline.

The pod does not receive a fresh 10 seconds starting from the second request.

Once SyncTerminatingPod succeeds, terminatedAt is set and the worker advances to TerminatedPod.


Relevant source: [`pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go at commit 400031d`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/400031d69530e018d5c001a922d3c5d2afaba954/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
